newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ forex market thumbs its nose at RBNZ's Brash.
newsitem.headline: NZ forex market thumbs its nose at RBNZ's Brash.

text.p: The New Zealand foreign exchange market on Wednesday responded to a call by the central bank governor for a lower exchange rate and higher interest rates by taking the Kiwi dollar higher.

Dealers said Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash was beating his head against the wall with his repeated calls. Higher interest rates, from an already high level in real terms, would always attract buying interest in the currency, they said.
"We will always have people chasing high yields if he continues to call for higher short term rates," said Bankers Trust dealer Philip Lindberg.
"Unless something changes, the market will probably say 'we'll buy dips and take the yield' and the Kiwi is going to edge a little bit higher."
By early afternoon the New Zealand dollar was at 69.7 U.S. cents compared with its 69.5 local close on Tuesday.
Brash told Reuters Financial TV in London that he would like a new mix of lower foreign exchange rates and higher interest rates to take the economy forward.
"I'd be much happier with a somewhat lower exchange rate and somewhat higher interest rates," said Brash in an interview.
"We've had a very strong rise in exchange rates and a fall in interest rates. Now I'd prefer to see a different combination," Brash said.
But dealers said they had heard it all before from Brash.
"The market knows his views and they are having less impact," said a Wellington bank dealer.
"Most people have a fundamental problem -- if you are going to have high interest rates you are not going to have a lower currency when you are supported by fairly sound fundamentals."

The debt market moved more in the direction Brash wants with indicator 90-day bank bill yields rising five basis points to 7.85 percent but dealers put that down to bearish sentiment and flows on the day rather than to Brash's comments.
They expect New Zealand's relatively high interest rates to attract fresh interest in eurokiwi and samurai issues.
"There is some expectation that we will see a re-emergence of interest from Japan in Kiwi and dual currency issues," said one dealer.

Monetary conditions are only marginally easier than in March when the RBNZ said they were too tight. The Bankers Trust Monetary Conditions Index was at 129 against 131 when the RBNZ made its easing call.
The market has kept conditions tight because growth has been stronger than the RBNZ had forecast and there are doubts that inflation pressures will fall as rapidly as the bank forecasts.
One chain holding the Kiwi back is wariness that the RBNZ will make another clear statement or signal that the market is keeping conditions too tight.
"Obviously people get the feeling the Reserve Bank are concerned, but the question is, do they do anything or do they let things continue on on their merry way," said Lindberg.
